passages.text: A multimodal manual therapy, exercise, and psychological intervention for painful diabetic neuropathy: the NeuOst feasibility randomised controlled trial
Supplemental Digital Content is Available in the Text.
A multimodal intervention for people with painful diabetic neuropathy proved feasible and acceptable in a feasibility trial, with encouraging clinical signals compared with usual care.
Abstract
Introduction:

People with painful diabetic neuropathy lack effective and tolerable treatments. <sentence_start/>Physical and psychological interventions may help but require further study and combination to maximise effects.
Objectives:

This single-site, 3-arm, parallel, randomised feasibility trial tested whether a multimodal intervention combining manual therapy, exercise, and psychologically informed conversations (“NeuOst”) was feasible, and a full-scale trial possible.
Methods:

Adults with painful diabetic neuropathy were randomised 1:1:1 to either (1) 5 individual sessions of NeuOst, (2) 5 sessions of a high-similarity control intervention with the same osteopaths, or (3) usual care. <sentence_start/>Allocation was computer-generated, and blinding was intended for assessors, research and administrative staff, and participants receiving NeuOst or the high-similarity control intervention. <sentence_start/>Feasibility and acceptability were assessed using predefined criteria. <sentence_start/>Exploratory clinical outcomes included pain, disability, and quality of life, collected up to 16 weeks post-randomisation.
Results:

Thirty-six participants were randomised; targets were met for eligibility (64%), consent (88%), retention (89%), blinding, fidelity, data completeness, and acceptability. <sentence_start/>Mean NeuOst session attendance was 82%, and satisfaction was high (mean 4.8/5). <sentence_start/>No serious adverse reactions occurred. <sentence_start/>Minor adverse responses were reported by 25% of NeuOst and 42% of control intervention participants. <sentence_start/>Recruitment rates indicated that modified procedures would be needed for a larger trial. <sentence_start/>Clinical outcomes were uncertain compared with control and promising compared with usual care.
Conclusion:

The NeuOst intervention was safe, acceptable, and feasible. <sentence_start/>The trial design proved largely workable, with areas for refinement identified. <sentence_start/>Findings support progression to an effectiveness trial.
1. Introduction

The global burden from painful diabetic polyneuropathy (pDPN) is increasing due to rising diabetes rates and ageing populations. <sentence_start/>Between 30% and 50% of individuals living with diabetes are estimated to experience diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN),<sup><citation rid="R24" ref-type="bibr" count="1">24</citation>,<citation rid="R72" ref-type="bibr" count="1">72</citation></sup> where nerve damage can lead to paraesthesia, numbness, and reduced thermal sensation, nociception, and proprioception.<citation rid="R1" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>1</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In diabetes, neurologial and microvascular compromise lead to ulcerations that can go undetected, leading to amputations and contributing to mortality.<sup><citation rid="R36" ref-type="bibr" count="1">36</citation>,<citation rid="R48" ref-type="bibr" count="1">48</citation></sup> Twenty-five percent or more of people with peripheral neuropathy also have neuropathic pain.<sup><citation rid="R44" ref-type="bibr" count="1">44</citation>,<citation rid="R72" ref-type="bibr" count="1">72</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>This is a highly distressing symptom, described by one of our patient partners as “walking on burning-hot sand and unable to get off it”<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> (a representative description).<citation rid="R8" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Neuropathy and pain not only affect physical functioning but also sleep, social relationships, and mental health.<sup><citation rid="R20" ref-type="bibr" count="1">20</citation>,<citation rid="R50" ref-type="bibr" count="1">50</citation>,<citation rid="R68" ref-type="bibr" count="1">68</citation></sup>

Current neuropathic pain care relies heavily on medications,<sup><citation rid="R17" ref-type="bibr" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="R57" ref-type="bibr" count="1">57</citation>,<citation rid="R59" ref-type="bibr" count="1">59</citation></sup> despite their limited efficacy and considerable side effects.<citation rid="R79" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>79</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Reflecting its impact, finding effective treatment options for painful DPN is a top priority for patients and health professionals.<sup><citation rid="R29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>,<citation rid="R65" ref-type="bibr" count="1">65</citation></sup> People with lived experience emphasise the additional need to consider neuropathy in the context of living with diabetes-itself a burdensome health challenge.<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation>

Physical and psychological interventions are potential alternatives for people experiencing neuropathic pain from DPN, allowing for person-centred care and consideration of biopsychosocial challenges. <sentence_start/>These interventions provide small-to-moderate symptom relief and quality of life gains in chronic pain conditions,<sup><citation rid="R13" ref-type="bibr" count="1">13</citation>,<citation rid="R85" ref-type="bibr" count="1">85</citation>,<citation rid="R93" ref-type="bibr" count="1">93</citation></sup> including neuropathic pain.<citation rid="R4" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>4</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Growing evidence shows benefits of exercise in DPN and other peripheral neuropathies, including for nerve fibre regeneration, symptomatic relief, quality of life, functional improvement, and blood glucose control<sup><citation rid="R2" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2</citation>,<citation rid="R45" ref-type="bibr" count="1">45</citation>,<citation rid="R53" ref-type="bibr" count="1">53</citation>,<citation rid="R73" ref-type="bibr" count="1">73</citation>,<citation rid="R75" ref-type="bibr" count="1">75</citation>,<citation rid="R81" ref-type="bibr" count="1">81</citation></sup> and suggests short-term effectiveness of manual therapy.<citation rid="R34" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>34</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Combinations of aerobic, strength, and balance training appear most promising,<sup><citation rid="R58" ref-type="bibr" count="1">58</citation>,<citation rid="R81" ref-type="bibr" count="1">81</citation></sup> although existing studies are often small and heterogeneous.<sup><citation rid="R46" ref-type="bibr" count="1">46</citation>,<citation rid="R61" ref-type="bibr" count="1">61</citation>,<citation rid="R71" ref-type="bibr" count="1">71</citation></sup> Because physical, psychological, and social challenges interact in pDPN, combinations of physical and psychological components may offer the most meaningful and sustainable outcomes. <sentence_start/>However, few multimodal interventions have been developed for individuals with pDPN.

We developed the multimodal intervention “NeuOst,” combining manual therapy, exercise, and psychologically informed strategies, delivered by specifically trained UK osteopathic manual therapists. <sentence_start/>Intervention development, content, and methods of the below feasibility trial are detailed elsewhere.<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Before evaluating treatment effects in a full-scale trial, key uncertainties and motivators for this study included the feasibility of delivering the NeuOst treatment as well as the feasibility of a randomised controlled trial (RCT). <sentence_start/>The primary objectives of this feasibility trial were thus to ascertain the feasibility of (1) delivering the NeuOst intervention and (2) conducting a 3-armed, parallel, partially blinded RCT of NeuOst as an adjunct to patients' usual care compared with a high-similarity control intervention<citation rid="R41" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>41</sup></citation> and compared with usual care only. <sentence_start/>To test feasibility, we prespecified feasibility outcomes as defined in the following section. <sentence_start/>We also gathered clinical outcome data-including harms-to inform future research steps but did not power the study to detect clinical changes.<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation>
2. Methods

This trial is reported in accordance with the 2025 CONSORT Statement<citation rid="R43" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>43</sup></citation> and CONSORT extensions for nonpharmacological therapies<citation rid="R9" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation> and pilot and feasibility trials.<citation rid="R25" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>25</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Interventions are described using TIDieR<citation rid="R37" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>37</sup></citation> and the CoPPS checklist for reporting of control interventions in efficacy and mechanistic trials of physical, psychological, and self-management therapies<citation rid="R41" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>41</sup></citation>-with completed reporting checklists appended (Supplemental Digital Content, SDC, ).
2.1. Preregistration

The trial was registered on on 15 May 2024 ( ), after enrolment of the first 4 participants (first participant enrolled on 30 April). <sentence_start/>Registration was completed following administrative delays during study start-up procedures. <sentence_start/>The study protocol and statistical analysis plan had been finalised before participant enrolment and remained unchanged until registration, and ethics approval had been obtained. <sentence_start/>No outcome data were accessed or analysed before trial registration. <sentence_start/>To enhance transparency, the full protocol and analysis plan were registered on the Open Science Framework on May 29, 2024 ( ).
2.2. <sentence_start/>Sponsor and ethics

The sponsor institution was the Health Sciences University (HSU)-UCO School of Osteopathy, and its institutional research ethics committee approved the study on 05 April 2024 (no identification numbers used by this committee).
2.3. Funders

The trial was funded by <italic>The Osteopathic Foundation</italic> and <italic>The Alan and Sheila Diamond Charitable Trust</italic>, with funders having had no role in the conduct, analysis, or write-up of the study.
2.4. <sentence_start/>Patient and public involvement

People with lived experience were consulted extensively during the development of the NeuOst intervention and were involved in the piloting of the control intervention and the training of providers-as described elsewhere.<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>During the trial, a permanent patient partner (E.P.) was part of the combined Trial Steering and Data Monitoring and Ethics Committee (TSC/DMEC). <sentence_start/>Results were discussed and interpreted with a board of 7 people with lived DPN experience, diverse regarding ethnicity, age, sex, language, and cultural background. <sentence_start/>Discussions informed this write-up, and E.P. co-authored this manuscript. <sentence_start/>Dissemination includes public events in the local community and direct communication with study participants.
2.5. <sentence_start/>Trial design

This was a prospective, randomised, parallel-arm, three-group, controlled, partially blinded, clinical feasibility trial, with a 16-week follow-up period and 1:1:1 allocation ratio (Fig. 1). <sentence_start/>The study was not powered to detect intervention effects, with clinical outcomes collected for exploratory reasons only.
Figure 1.

Design of the NeuOst feasibility trial. <sentence_start/>Interventions are described in detail in the manuscript text and the published protocol, with “control intervention” referring to a specifically designed intervention replicating the tested (“NeuOst”) intervention but omitting components the effects of which were to be studied in the trial. <sentence_start/>All 3 trial groups continued their usual care outside the trial. <sentence_start/>BL, baseline assessment; F-U, follow-up assessment; Recruit., recruitment; Screen., screening.
2.6. <sentence_start/>Trial setting

The trial was conducted in London, United Kingdom, at a single outpatient site: the teaching clinic of the sponsor institution (postcode SE1). <sentence_start/>Treatments were provided in individual rooms, equipped with a treatment plinth and seating.
2.7. <sentence_start/>Recruitment and consent

Between April and December 2024, patient recruitment was conducted through a multichannel strategy including local print and online media (5 adverts), institutional newsletters (7, including 1 to 10,000 members), and at least 12 social media posts. <sentence_start/>Flyers were distributed across more than 30 sites, mainly in South-East London, including clinics, libraries, pharmacies, churches, and community centres, with additional direct outreach to UK National Health Service (NHS) diabetes and General Practitioner (GP) teams, local charities, and community organisations. <sentence_start/>Note that recruitment strategies did not include formal NHS recruitment such as identification of potential participants from health records or during routine appointments. <sentence_start/>Instead, we only used flyers in public spaces of relevant NHS services (GP and intermediate care diabetes services). <sentence_start/>Towards the end of the year, connections were also made with local community champions active in diabetes advocacy.
2.8. <sentence_start/>Eligibility criteria
2.8.1. <sentence_start/>Participants

Adults with pDPN were eligible, irrespective of most comorbidities and medication use. <sentence_start/>Participants had to have a diagnosis of diabetes, and score ≥4 points on the Michigan Neuropathy Screening Instrument (MNSI, questionnaire part)-indicating likely peripheral diabetic neuropathy based on patient-reported symptoms.<citation rid="R33" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Second, a score of ≥3 was required for the Douleur Neuropathique 4 (DN4, interview part), evaluating typical patient-reported pain descriptors and associated symptoms typical for neuropathic pain, and applied to the legs or feet.<citation rid="R80" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>80</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>To simplify recruitment processes, we screened patients using phone interviews and did not use physical examinations to determine eligibility.

Patients were ineligible if manual therapy and conservative pain management were contraindicated, if they had past or scheduled amputations, or if changes to exercise or pain management regimens had been made in the past month or were planned for the next 3 months. <sentence_start/>To facilitate blinding, we also excluded patients who reported knowing any other trial participants. <sentence_start/>For details and a full list of criteria, see the public trial protocol ( ).
2.8.2. <sentence_start/>Providers and provider training

Trial providers were fully qualified, registered osteopaths with at least 1 year's clinical experience but no prior expertise with neuropathy or diabetes populations. <sentence_start/>Providers had to have received training to deliver the NeuOst and the control intervention as part of an expert-delivered training course and pretrial methodological workshops. <sentence_start/>The intervention training course encompassed at least 7 hours of self-study through recorded lectures and reading materials and 8 hours of in-person practical training. <sentence_start/>Competency was assessed through quizzes and observation after the course, and providers received regular supervision during the trial (training and supervision described in <citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Ref. 40</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition, trial-specific methodological provider training included education about RCT methods, the purpose of control interventions and blinding, control intervention co-design, and practical training with patient partners in NeuOst and control intervention delivery.
2.8.3. <sentence_start/>Settings
No specific eligibility criteria existed for settings.
2.9. <sentence_start/>Intervention and comparators
All study arms are described in detail in the preregistered protocol ( )<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> and in supplementary treatment manuals (SDC, ).
2.9.1. <sentence_start/>NeuOst intervention (tested intervention)

The intervention, NeuOst, was developed following the MRC framework for complex interventions,<citation rid="R76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.17863/CAM.77753" count="1"><sup>76</sup></citation> using a logic model informed by literature, expert input, patient involvement, and iterative testing. <sentence_start/>Content was refined through multidisciplinary collaboration and feedback from people with lived experience.<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation>

NeuOst combines manual therapy techniques with psychologically informed pain management derived from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy,<citation rid="R56" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>56</sup></citation> and exercise rehabilitation, plus neurological testing as well as diabetes and foot care education and screening. <sentence_start/>Fully qualified osteopaths delivered NeuOst in up to 5 one-to-one sessions, with the first session lasting 90 minutes and followed by four 60-minute sessions. <sentence_start/>All sessions were guided by a treatment manual that specified core and optional components, dosage, and personalisation options.

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT)-derived elements were structured around weekly worksheets with scripted ACT-derived experiential/reflective exercises and metaphors (see SDC, ), including those aimed at fostering present-moment awareness, openness, values exploration, and values-based goal setting-completed in conversation with providers. <sentence_start/>Of note, while this element of the intervention was guided by principles of ACT, it was not intended to be a complete ACT intervention. <sentence_start/>Five supervision sessions with the trial clinical psychologist, W.S., and the providers were conducted. <sentence_start/>These focused on reflection, supporting clinicians' conversations with patients in an ACT-consistent manner and managing challenges arising during the delivery of ACT-derived strategies.

Manual therapy included prolonged articulation of lower-extremity joints, active-resisted muscle activation, soft tissue mobilisation, and neurodynamic techniques. <sentence_start/>Although delivered by osteopaths, the core techniques of the manual therapy protocol were delivered in a manner not specific to any particular manual therapy profession.<citation rid="R22" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation>

Exercise elements were practised with participants in clinic and performed during a progressive home-exercise programme. <sentence_start/>An inflatable balance cushion was provided to each participant. <sentence_start/>Participants were instructed to perform the stretch, strength, and stability elements of the programme at least once per day and engage in a personalised amount and intensity of cardiovascular activity 3 times per week, agreed through values-based goal setting with providers. <sentence_start/>Participants received a printed exercise programme, including for daily activity tracking.
Printed leaflets were also provided and used to support conversations on the importance of foot care and exercise in diabetes.
2.9.2. <sentence_start/>Control intervention

The control intervention was delivered by the same set of trial providers. <sentence_start/>It aimed at blinding participants and all staff (except providers) to NeuOst vs control intervention allocation, and at creating comparable placebo effects to enable efficacy testing of the NeuOst treatment. <sentence_start/>It was designed according to best-practice guidance,<citation rid="R41" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>41</sup></citation> and developed and piloted with providers and patient partners. <sentence_start/>The control was designed to match the NeuOst intervention in the following features: number, duration and frequency of sessions, assessment procedures, protocol standardisation and flexibility, opportunities for intervention tailoring and participant participation, application modes (conversational, manual, and self-performed physical), delivery formats, thematic content of conversations and informational material, body areas addressed, physical procedures performed or undergone and sensations experienced (with below exceptions), equipment employed, fidelity monitoring methods, treatment environment, personal interactions with staff and providers, provider characteristics and behaviour, follow-up frequency and mode, and co-interventions (education, foot and neurological screening) (see SDC, for detail).

The following components differed and were thus supposed to be tested by this trial design: NeuOst activities derived from ACT were replaced by generic discussions of a patient's pain experience and their current self-management strategies, structured around specifically developed worksheets to resemble the ones used to deliver ACT activities. <sentence_start/>Manual therapy techniques were applied with reduced range and minimal force, and neurodynamic techniques with reduced range. <sentence_start/>Exercise promotion was limited to education and exploration of exercise barriers, the provision of an inflatable balance cushion-which was also provided in the NeuOst arm-and advice about specific exercises as per therapist preference but was not structured through a formal exercise plan.

This control intervention design sought to avoid core ACT mechanisms related to psychological flexibility (behaviour that is “aware, open, and engaged”), limit the activation of joint receptors through end-of-range movement, relaxation of muscles, or mobilisation of nerves, and avoid promoting behaviour change toward engagement in a structured programme of progressive aerobic and anaerobic physical activity.

We sought to reduce group contamination by not recruiting participants who knew of other study participants (assessed through patient self-report) and by avoiding overlapping appointment times. <sentence_start/>All providers had co-developed the control intervention and were trained-including in the scientific rationale for control interventions and blinding (SDC, ). <sentence_start/>Further details and a description of intervention similarity are provided in <citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Reference 40</citation>.
2.9.3. <sentence_start/>Usual care

Control and NeuOst interventions were delivered as an adjunct to patients' usual care, which participants continued outside the trial. <sentence_start/>Participants randomised to the dedicated usual care arm did not receive care as part of the trial and only participated in outcome collection calls.
All participants were asked not to change their medical or nonpharmacological pain or neuropathy care routine although doing so did not lead to withdrawal from the study.
2.10. <sentence_start/>Fidelity promotion and monitoring

Fidelity to NeuOst and control intervention protocols was measured by a provider-completed checklist for each attended session (SDC, ). <sentence_start/>Resource constraints prevented the independent verification of intervention delivery. <sentence_start/>At regular supervision sessions with the chief investigator (D.H.S.) and trial psychologist (W.S.), challenges with NeuOst and control intervention delivery were discussed, and delivery harmonised where possible. <sentence_start/>Participant adherence to interventions was not enhanced beyond routine encouragement from clinicians and check-in calls if appointments were missed. <sentence_start/>To assess the content of “usual care,” healthcare utilisation in the usual care arm was evaluated through patient report (as it was in all other arms).
2.11. <sentence_start/>Outcomes and data collection timepoints
2.11.1. <sentence_start/>Feasibility outcomes

Feasibility was judged according to several feasibility outcomes, following prespecified criteria (see protocol<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> and section 3). <sentence_start/>Feasibility outcomes were rates of the following:
(1) Eligibility
(2) Recruitment
(3) Consent
(4) Blinding
(5) Intervention fidelity in treatment delivery
(6) Data completeness
(7) Participant retention
(8) Adverse events
(9) Treatment acceptability (through satisfaction ratings, session attendance rates, and qualitative feedback)
Most feasibility outcome data, such as attendance of clinical sessions or outcome assessments, were collected continuously through study administrative logs.
Blinding was assessed after the final treatment visit, and intervention acceptability and satisfaction were assessed after the final visit and the final follow-up (week 16).
2.11.2. <sentence_start/>Clinical and exploratory outcomes

Clinical outcome data were collected through phone or video calls with blinded outcome assessors at the following timepoint: at baseline, after the final treatment session (or at week 5 for usual care arm participants, 3 weeks thereafter [week 8], and after another 8 weeks [week 16; all through calls] [Fig. 1 and protocol]).<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Participants received £15 per completed study assessment call. <sentence_start/>The longest follow-up was approximately 16 weeks after randomisation.

For the 2 groups attending clinic appointments (NeuOst and control intervention), clinical outcomes were also collected before each clinical visit using patient self-report on paper case report forms.

Owing to the feasibility nature of the trial, clinical outcomes were secondary, collected to evaluate their suitability as primary outcome measures in a full-scale trial. <sentence_start/>This objective also explains the partial overlap, eg, between some disability and quality of life measures. <sentence_start/>Collected clinical outcomes were as follows:
(1) Patient-reported pain severity and interference (measured using the Brief Pain Inventory, short form)<citation rid="R83" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>83</sup></citation>

(2) Disability (Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathic Pain Impact measure [DPNPI])<sup><citation rid="R10" ref-type="bibr" count="1">10</citation>,<citation rid="R11" ref-type="bibr" count="1">11</citation></sup>
(3) Neuropathy-specific quality of life (Neuropathy- and foot ulcer-specific quality of life instrument [NeuroQoL])<citation rid="R89" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>89</sup></citation>
(4) Fear of falling (Falls Efficacy Scale International, Falls Efficacy Scale (FES-I), 7-item short form [Tinetti et al., 1990])<citation rid="R86" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>86</sup></citation>

(5) Number of days with “bothersome” and “intolerable” pain in past week (approach adapted from<sup><citation rid="R31" ref-type="bibr" count="1">31</citation>,<citation rid="R64" ref-type="bibr" count="1">64</citation></sup> and [Markman et al., 2020])<citation rid="R54" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>54</sup></citation>
(6) Physical activity levels (trial-specific exercise compliance form)
(7) Global impression of change (Patient's Global Impression of Change scale [Dworkin et al., 2005])<citation rid="R23" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation>
(8) Concomitant medication and intervention use (using a form adapted from NIH NCCIH Prior and Concomitant Medications and Interventions Form)

Furthermore, healthcare utilisation and receipt of concomitant care were monitored during assessment calls in all groups-including health education, physical and psychological care, and performance of exercise.

To explore participants' physical activity levels and as a potential indicator of adherence to the exercise programme, we collected data on activity levels at each follow-up timepoint, including before each clinic visit of the NeuOst and control intervention groups. <sentence_start/>Data were collected as participant-reported time spent doing either any strength, stretch, or stability exercises, or any cardiovascular activity.

Expectations and treatment credibility were assessed to supplement blinding data. <sentence_start/>Data were collected at baseline (ie, before randomisation and based on information available to participants at that time about the NeuOst intervention, eg, from the Participant Information Sheet) and at visit 2 in the NeuOst and control intervention arms (ie, after 1 exposure to the allocated intervention). <sentence_start/>To do so, we used the Credibility and Expectancy Questionnaire<sup><citation rid="R7" ref-type="bibr" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="R21" ref-type="bibr" count="1">21</citation></sup> and the Stanford Expectations of Treatment Scale (SETS).<citation rid="R96" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>96</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The Credibility and Expectancy Questionnaire was analysed by converting percentage scores of items 4 and 6 into 1 to 9 Likert format ((X/100) × 8 + 1) and by averaging the credibility items (1-3) and expectancy items (4-6) to obtain subscores, with higher scores indicating higher credibility and expectancy, respectively. <sentence_start/>Assessed using the SETS, positive and negative treatment expectations were calculated as means of SETS items 1, 3, and 5 and 2, 4, and 6, respectively, with values ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree), with 4 meaning “neither agree nor disagree.”<citation rid="R96" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>96</sup></citation> SETS item 10 was framed to evaluate if participants had experienced “osteopathy” before.
2.12. Harms

Adverse events and reactions were defined in the protocol, including their severity and potential relation to study procedures. <sentence_start/>Participants were asked systematically about any adverse health changes at each clinical appointment and each outcome assessment, in addition to being able to report harms to the study team by phone and email as they occurred.
2.13. <sentence_start/>Sample size and power

Twelve participants per arm was considered to be the minimum number to make meaningful inferences about key feasibility parameters and to assess variance of clinical effects and inform progression to a full-scale trial.<citation rid="R14" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation>
The study was not powered to detect statistically significant differences in effects between intervention arms, and no conclusions about clinical effects should be drawn.
2.14. <sentence_start/>Randomisation

Blocked randomisation was used throughout enrolment and at the end of the trial to ensure balance in the number of participants across the 3 trial arms (1:1:1 allocation ratio). <sentence_start/>Random permuted block sizes of 3 or 6 participants were used in an unpredictable order to limit predictability of allocations. <sentence_start/>Participants were randomised by a researcher after enrolment and upon completion of baseline assessments. <sentence_start/>The randomisation sequence was generated by the web-based system <italic>Sealed Envelope</italic> (Sealed Envelope Ltd, London, United Kingdom), providing single allocation codes at each randomisation event and preventing researcher influence over group allocation. <sentence_start/>To maintain blinding, coded labels were used to inform treatment providers of assignments, the meaning of which was known only to providers. <sentence_start/>The key for decoding was kept by a colleague not directly involved in the research. <sentence_start/>The code was broken once an initial blinded analysis had been performed on the complete dataset, and results had been verified by the chief investigator and shared with the independent TSC/DMEC.
2.15. <sentence_start/>Blinding

Participants, outcome assessors, and data analysts were blinded to the nature of assigned interventions, except for assignment to the usual care arm (not blinded). <sentence_start/>Intervention providers were not blinded.

Blinding was attempted by using a high-similarity control intervention, following current guidance.<citation rid="R41" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>41</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Designed to replicate the NeuOst test intervention except for key components of interest, which were removed or altered, the control intervention aimed to produce comparable expectations, mirror context factors, and blind participants and research and administrative staff to group allocations. <sentence_start/>Providers were specifically trained about the importance of maintaining blinding-as were all other staff-and in the delivery of the control intervention (SDC, ).
2.16. <sentence_start/>Statistical methods and analysis

A detailed statistical analysis plan (SAP) was developed before enrolment, focusing on descriptive statistics for demographic variables and primary (feasibility) outcomes. <sentence_start/>Categorical data were analysed as frequencies, proportions, and percentages, while continuous data were presented as means and standard deviations (SD).

For feasibility outcomes, progression rules were prespecified (see section 3), including criteria to proceed, amend the study design, or consider aborting progression to a full-scale trial with the present methodology (SAP available at ).
Data analyses were performed in R (version 4.5.2) using RStudio (version 2026.01.0+392) for clinical measures and in STATA (version 13) or Excel for feasibility data.

The only feasibility outcome for which a (prespecified) between-group test was performed was blinding: Bang blinding index (BI) was calculated for the NeuOst and control intervention groups, respectively. <sentence_start/>Scaled to an interval of −1 to 1, a BI of 1 indicates complete lack of blinding in the control intervention group (correct allocation guessing), 0 is deemed consistent with perfect blinding or chance guessing, and −1 indicates opposite guessing (ie, control intervention participants believing to have received the NeuOst study treatment). <sentence_start/>The ratio of allocation guesses between groups was calculated as a standardised mean difference (Hedges g), re-coding BI directionality in 1 study arm as per Colagiuri et al.,<citation rid="R15" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation> and compared using a random effects model. <sentence_start/>In the absence of accepted best practice to compare blinding assessments between study arms,<sup><citation rid="R41" ref-type="bibr" count="1">41</citation>,<citation rid="R95" ref-type="bibr" count="1">95</citation></sup> Bang blinding indices were also compared between groups using a χ<sup>2</sup> test.<citation rid="R15" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation>

As the study was not powered to test efficacy, no formal statistical hypothesis testing was conducted on clinical or safety outcomes. <sentence_start/>Instead, mean changes from baseline to follow-up for each outcome and group were calculated (SDC, ). <sentence_start/>Secondary descriptive analyses explored clinical changes in key candidates for future primary outcome measures. <sentence_start/>The pain severity and interference subscales of the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) were chosen for these exploratory analyses because of the BPI's widespread use and validation in pain research,<citation rid="R28" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>28</sup></citation> its sensitivity to change,<citation rid="R47" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>47</sup></citation> and coherence with NeuOst intervention theory.<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Calculated using analysis of covariance adjusted for baseline values, we present BPI between-group differences with a range of confidence intervals (75% to 95%) in forest plots, with zero-difference and minimally important clinical differences (MCID) marked. <sentence_start/>In this study, a difference of 1.2 points was deemed clinically important for efficacy (NeuOst vs control intervention)<sup><citation rid="R70" ref-type="bibr" count="1">70</citation>,<citation rid="R78" ref-type="bibr" count="1">78</citation></sup> and 2.0 for effectiveness comparisons (NeuOst vs usual care).<citation rid="R55" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>55</sup></citation>

All analyses were conducted using all available data as randomised. <sentence_start/>Deviating from our protocol, missing data were not imputed, recognising the feasibility-focused and descriptive nature of the clinical outcome data analysis in this study. <sentence_start/>Additional per-protocol sensitivity analyses included only data from participants who received the intervention they had been assigned to and who attended at least 3 of the 5 intervention sessions (except when in the usual care arm).
No interim analyses or stopping rules were planned or implemented.
2.17. <sentence_start/>Changes to trial protocol and protocol deviations

A protocol amendment specified that renal failure would only lead to ineligibility if requiring hospital-based dialysis; We had found that contemporary peritoneal dialysis is commonly performed at home and was unlikely to interfere with study participation.

Deviating from the original plan, resource limitations prevented us from video recording a subset of treatment sessions or monitoring fidelity with an independent assessor. <sentence_start/>Instead, we relied solely on provider report, who, at each session, marked all delivered treatment and control intervention elements in their treatment manuals. <sentence_start/>For 2 participants randomised to the NeuOst intervention, trial providers inadvertently used the control intervention manual to document intervention fidelity and care delivery. <sentence_start/>This appears to have resulted from a distribution error by clinic administrative staff. <sentence_start/>Although this affected the accuracy of fidelity documentation for these cases, our review indicates that the participants nevertheless received the intended NeuOst intervention. <sentence_start/>Unplanned sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the impact of this error.

Data on healthcare utilisation and concomitant medication use were only collected at baseline to determine the feasibility of collecting such data. <sentence_start/>Follow-up data were not collected to reduce research burden. <sentence_start/>Physical foot exams were performed by providers at baseline for clinical orientation and patient communication only, and not to confirm eligibility as originally planned because, by then, participants had been enrolled and randomised.
2.18. <sentence_start/>Open science and data access
A full protocol, SAP, and the final, anonymised dataset are freely available on the Open Science Framework (OSF, ).
3. Results
3.1. <sentence_start/>Participant flow and CONSORT diagram

We enrolled the target of 36 participants. <sentence_start/>Twelve participants were randomised to each study group. <sentence_start/>Of those, 1 participant in the control intervention arm never attended a session, and 2 patients in the NeuOst arm discontinued treatment after 2 of the 5 sessions. <sentence_start/>Further detail on retention and adherence is provided in the feasibility analysis below and in Figure 2.
Figure 2.
Participant flow diagram as per CONSORT guidance.
3.2. <sentence_start/>Sample characteristics at baseline

The recruited sample had diverse ethnic, linguistic, educational, and economic backgrounds. <sentence_start/>The average age was 64.2 years (SD 13.3), most participants were overweight or obese, and half lived with additional long-term conditions to diabetes and DPN (Table 1).
3.3. <sentence_start/>Provider characteristics

Six providers treated at least 1 patient as part of the trial. <sentence_start/>Providers were UK-registered osteopaths; 3 women and 3 men. <sentence_start/>At the start of the trial, they had spent 1 to 7 years in clinical practice (median 1.5 years' experience).
3.4. <sentence_start/>Primary analysis: feasibility and acceptability

Most prespecified criteria for progression were met, except for recruitment, where a modified strategy would be needed in a full-scale trial (Table 2). <sentence_start/>One analysis of blinding also did not meet all predefined success criteria, although this indicated unbalanced blinding between groups as opposed to a lack of blinding in any of the 2 relevant study arms.
3.4.1. <sentence_start/>Recruitment, eligibility, and consent rates
The target number of 36 participants was recruited in approx. <sentence_start/>9 months, from April 1, 2024 to January 3, 2025, meaning an average of 4 participants were recruited per calendar month.

Over this period, contact was made with 82 individuals, of whom 62 (76%) were formally screened, with 41 (66%) of those screened deemed eligible. <sentence_start/>Of the 41 participants screened as eligible, 88% (36) consented to trial participation (Table 2; Fig. 2).

Ineligibility was largely due to the absence of neuropathic pain (20%) or DPN (17%) as per DN4 and MNSI questionnaire assessments, and no or unclear diabetes (15%), followed by ineligible comorbidities, lack of foot pain, and unstable medication regimens.

Most patients contacted the study team after learning about the study through a local diabetes clinic network (n = 16) or through word of mouth (n = 10). <sentence_start/>Flyers accounted for 24 contacts across podiatry clinics, private clinics, the HSU-UCO trial site, other NHS sites, public spaces, and unspecified locations. <sentence_start/>Additional sources included emails from clinics/organisations (n = 10), newspapers (n = 3), social media (n = 2), the study newsletter (n = 1), and onward referrals from another study (n = 5).
3.4.2. <sentence_start/>Treatment completion and study retention rates

Participants attended an average of 86% of treatment sessions (across NeuOst and control intervention groups) (103/120). <sentence_start/>Participants in the NeuOst group attended 82% of their sessions (49/60, or 4.1 of 5 sessions per participant, Table 2)-with 2 participants only attending 2 sessions each. <sentence_start/>In the control intervention, attendance was 90% (54/60, or 4.5 sessions per participant)-with 1 participant not attending any sessions.

Four participants dropped out of the trial (11% attrition), ie, also stopped attending data collection calls: 3 due to unknown reasons and lost contact (1 in each study arm), and 1 due to personal circumstances interfering with trial participation (in the NeuOst arm) (Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>The attrition rate in the NeuOst arm was thus 17% (Table 2).
3.4.3. <sentence_start/>Data completeness

Participants who attended assessment calls always responded to all required questions. <sentence_start/>Missing data were thus calculated simply as the proportion of missed assessment calls, rather than data points. <sentence_start/>Missed data collections ranged from 8% to 17% per group and follow-up timepoint, with no notable differences between groups or time points (SDC Table S1, ). <sentence_start/>The total rate of missing data across all groups and the 3 follow-up time points was 12%.
3.4.4. <sentence_start/>Acceptability and satisfaction

At the final point of follow-up, participants were asked several feedback questions about their experience in the study. <sentence_start/>Overall, satisfaction with trial organisation and clinical care was high across groups. <sentence_start/>Almost all participants indicated they would participate in a larger study and would recommend to others to participate in a similar study (Table 3).

Responses to open-ended feedback questions indicated that participants generally found the trial acceptable and the interventions beneficial (SDC Table S2, ). <sentence_start/>Participants also valued personal contact and relationships with providers, manual therapy, and scheduling flexibility. <sentence_start/>Feedback highlighted difficulties with outcome questionnaires, occasional uncertainties about procedures, frustration with not receiving trial-related care in the usual care group, and practical participation barriers. <sentence_start/>Suggestions were made for improved communication, simplified outcome assessments, and longer or more frequent intervention sessions.
3.4.5. <sentence_start/>Interventionist fidelity in treatment delivery

During 87% of intervention sessions in the NeuOst arm, providers delivered over 80% of mandatory treatment protocol items, as measured by a provider-completed treatment checklist. <sentence_start/>Errors in distributing treatment documentation materials meant that treatments were documented with the wrong case report form for 2 participants in the NeuOst arm (affecting a total of 7 sessions). <sentence_start/>When excluding these sessions from the treatment fidelity analysis, the proportion of high-fidelity NeuOst sessions was 95%.

The treatment handbook also included optional protocol items, of which an average range of 4% to 9% were delivered per session. <sentence_start/>Here, the most delivered optional component in the NeuOst arm was making modifications to the exercise programme to meet patient needs. <sentence_start/>Detailed fidelity data are provided in the SDC (Table S3, ).
3.4.6. <sentence_start/>Treatment credibility, expectations, and blinding assessments
Results of treatment expectation and credibility assessments are reported in Table 4. <sentence_start/>Although not tested statistically, no marked differences between the groups were noted.
3.4.6.1. <sentence_start/>Blinding group guesses at immediate follow-up

Immediately after the intervention period, participants were asked to guess which of the 3 study groups they were in. <sentence_start/>Their guesses are shown in Table 5. <sentence_start/>Although an equal number of participants in the NeuOst and in the control intervention arm believed to have received the (NeuOst) study treatment, more people in the NeuOst arm believed to have had the control intervention, and more control intervention participants were unsure.
3.4.6.1.1. <sentence_start/>Bang blinding index

Group guesses were compared with BI. <sentence_start/>Bang blinding index in the NeuOst arm was 0.27 (−0.24 to 0.78, 95% confidence interval, CI; n = 11), indicating a tendency towards correct guessing in this arm, but with random guessing (i.e., BI = 0) well within the 95% CI. <sentence_start/>Bang blinding index in the control intervention group was −0.45 (−0.84 to −0.07, 95% CI; n = 11), meaning patients tended towards guessing their allocation incorrectly in this group, believing they received the “real” intervention. <sentence_start/>The confidence interval does not include chance guessing.
3.4.6.1.2. <sentence_start/>Hedges g of Bang blinding indices

Hedges g was used to quantify the differences in blinding guesses between NeuOst and control intervention groups. <sentence_start/>It was g = 3.15 (3.02-3.28, 95% CI), <italic>P</italic> < 0.01, indicating that a larger proportion of patients in the control intervention arm thought they received active treatment or did not know which intervention they received than in the NeuOst arm (Table 5).
3.4.6.1.3. <sentence_start/>Chi-squared test comparing group guesses

The χ<sup>2</sup> test, used to compare raw guessing data rather than blinding indices, indicated no significant difference in allocation guessing between the NeuOst and control intervention groups (χ<sup>2</sup>[2, n = 22] = 1.67, <italic>P</italic> = 0.37).
3.4.6.1.4. <sentence_start/>Reasons for group guesses

Participants were asked to justify their group guesses. <sentence_start/>The reasons for guessing that a “real” treatment had been received-irrespective of the actual intervention received-related to (1) the perceived authenticity of the experience, (2) clinical effects or the care being perceived as overall helpful, and (3) participants recognising intervention components as familiar (SDC, Table S4, ).

Some reasons given for group guesses were difficult to reconcile with the direction of the guess. <sentence_start/>For example, 1 NeuOst-arm participant guessed they were in the control intervention group because the sessions met their expected level of massage and discussion, while another felt the practitioner's activities were familiar and unsurprising. <sentence_start/>The use of familiar components in NeuOst may have reduced novelty and thus contributed to successful blinding. <sentence_start/>Another participant, also guessing control, perceived the sessions as largely conversational and monitoring-focused rather than a “real” treatment with “actual discussions or prescription of medications,” highlighting how violated/unrealistic expectations may produce incorrect guesses.

Control group participants who believed they received the NeuOst treatment cited the intensity and thoroughness of the sessions, hands-on techniques, psychological support, exercises, and improvements in pain and mobility as reasons for their belief. <sentence_start/>Psychological support, clinician attention, and diagnostic conversations also contributed to this perception.
3.4.7. <sentence_start/>Adverse events

Three patients (25%) in the NeuOst intervention arm experienced at least 1 <italic>trial-related</italic> adverse response, with 5 (42%) in the control intervention and none (0%) in the usual care arm. <sentence_start/>All trial-related events were mild, except 1 post-treatment leg pain episode in the control intervention arm rated as 'severe'. <sentence_start/>No serious trial-related reactions occurred (Table 6).
3.5. <sentence_start/>Secondary outcomes (clinical measures)

We successfully collected data for the BPI, the number of days with bothersome and intolerable DPN symptoms in the past week, NeuroQoL, the DPNPI, and the FES-I. Descriptive inspection of scores across follow-up timepoints suggested that values were often lower than baseline across all these measures in both the NeuOst and the control intervention group-a pattern not observed in the UC group. <sentence_start/>This included suggested benefits in the NeuroQoL and DPNPI domains relating to symptom severity and frequency, mobility/physical function, sleep, emotional distress, daily activities, and social function (SDC, Table S5, ).

Additional descriptive analyses were performed for the Brief Pain Inventory's severity and interference domains and for the item “worst pain in the past week.” <sentence_start/>The spaghetti plots in Figure 3 provide a similar picture of nondifferentiation between NeuOst and the control intervention, but separation from the symptom development in the usual care arm, especially at the first 2 follow-up timepoints (immediately after the end of the treatment period and 3 weeks later).

Across all 3 follow-up timepoints, 60% to 90% of participants in the NeuOst and the control intervention groups reported their overall health status to be minimally, much, or very much improved compared with the beginning of this study. <sentence_start/>In the usual care arm, only 20% to 36% of participants did so, and most (57%-80%) reported no change or some worsening (Fig. 8). <sentence_start/>Numerical data are provided in the SDC (Table S6, ).

Healthcare utilisation data were only collected at baseline. <sentence_start/>Patients reported having used an average of 1.6 healthcare services in the preceding 4 weeks (SD 1.3) (SDC Table S7, ). <sentence_start/>Across all 36 patients, this included 12 patients consulting with GPs, 14 seeing a diabetes nurse, and 13 attending specialist services. <sentence_start/>Only 5 (14%) consulted no healthcare services at all in the past month.

Medication use was collected through patient self-report. <sentence_start/>Given the time requirements and challenges involved in verbally collecting such data through phone or video calls-especially from patients with long medication lists-the research team resorted to asking for medication lists to be sent through email. <sentence_start/>This resulted in considerable additional administrative burden, suggesting a different approach to data collection would be needed in a full-scale trial. <sentence_start/>Data are not presented here.

Figure 9 describes participant-reported time spent doing either any strength, stretch, or stability exercises, or any cardiovascular activity. <sentence_start/>Spaghetti plots and data tables are provided in the SDC (Tables S8 and S9; Figures S1 and S2, ). <sentence_start/>Although not tested formally, the data indicate no major changes in activity levels either within or between groups. <sentence_start/>Data variance around means was considerable.

Sensitivity analyses of the BPI data exploration were performed with a per-protocol sample, only including participants who attended at least 3 NeuOst or control intervention sessions. <sentence_start/>Although not presented here in detail, results did not differ notably. <sentence_start/>No further subgrouping was deemed relevant or feasible, also due to small sample sizes.
4. Discussion

This study demonstrated the feasible delivery and high acceptability of a novel intervention for people with painful diabetic neuropathy, combining manual therapy techniques, staged exercises, and psychologically informed conversations, alongside assessments, education, and complication screening by Allied Health professionals.<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The diverse pDPN sample was highly satisfied and adherent. <sentence_start/>The three-armed RCT was largely feasible, comparing the NeuOst intervention to a blinded high-similarity control intervention and nonblinded usual care. <sentence_start/>Key feasibility markers were met, although recruitment procedures need modification for a larger trial. <sentence_start/>Mild adverse responses were common, but no serious adverse reactions occurred.
4.1. <sentence_start/>Feasibility measures

Methodologically, the study design appeared promising, meeting criteria for eligibility, consent, retention, blinding, fidelity, data completeness, and study acceptability. <sentence_start/>Recruitment was challenging using mainly public advertising, although advertising in NHS spaces helped. <sentence_start/>Future trials should recruit directly through diabetes services and existing patient lists. <sentence_start/>Participant feedback and the long duration of outcome collection calls indicated a need to simplify data collection-using less burdensome measures, especially for disability and quality of life, and obtaining healthcare utilisation data from electronic records. <sentence_start/>Better methods are also needed for exercise monitoring, and more resources for independent fidelity monitoring.

The control intervention was designed to mimic NeuOst and blind participants and research staff to allocation, building on methodological guidance.<citation rid="R41" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>41</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Close collaboration with trial providers and patient partners was key to its success, fostering provider buy-in and confidence through co-design and training.<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Problems arose from the practical complexities of communicating using allocation codes and confusingly similar sets of treatment manuals. <sentence_start/>More piloting, closer supervision, and limited involvement of an unblinded researcher may have mitigated these challenges. <sentence_start/>Clinical results point to another concern with high-similarity control interventions: Although not powered to detect clinical effects, outcome differences between the NeuOst and its control intervention were smaller than those compared with usual care-if present at all. <sentence_start/>Of note, expectation measures were comparable between all 3 groups and blinding was likely effective. <sentence_start/>This comparison of NeuOst to its high-similarity control intervention prompts reconsideration of the intervention theory: Matched components such as validation, education, touch, personalised care, and attention may play central roles for clinical effects.<citation rid="R39" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>39</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In a full trial, we will intensify key NeuOst intervention components. <sentence_start/>If designing an efficacy trial, we will ensure that theoretically active treatment components are distinctly absent from the control intervention-including through better fidelity monitoring or a stepped-wedge cluster design. <sentence_start/>Overall, the methodological success of a credible blinded control intervention brings 4.2. <sentence_start/>Clinical outcomes

Clinically, the study underscores the potential value of person-centred, multimodal nonpharmacological care for people with pDPN.<citation rid="R88" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>88</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Clinical changes were encouraging-particularly shortly after the intervention period and contrasted with usual care. <sentence_start/>However, variability was large, no difference was apparent compared with the high-similarity control intervention, and the small sample prevented firm conclusions.

Compared with usual care, NeuOst showed preliminary and exploratory signals of improvement across all collected outcomes, including symptom severity, interference with function and emotional wellbeing (BPI, NeuroQoL, and DPNPI), fear of falling (FES-I), and patients' global impression of change. <sentence_start/>Days with “bothersome” symptoms also potentially decreased in both intervention groups. <sentence_start/>This breadth of possible effects corresponds to NeuOst's intervention theory, which postulated multiple target mechanisms across psychological, behavioural, and physical domains.<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Theorised therapeutic outcomes were correspondingly broad and included quality of life, fear of falling, and healthcare utilisation. <sentence_start/>Pain and symptom severity were not key targets but may also have improved.

exercise.<sup><citation rid="R66" ref-type="bibr" count="1">66</citation>,<citation rid="R84" ref-type="bibr" count="1">84</citation>,<citation rid="R92" ref-type="bibr" count="1">92</citation></sup> Here, lessons can be learnt from combined approaches in back pain and musculoskeletal research.<sup><citation rid="R16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation>,<citation rid="R85" ref-type="bibr" count="1">85</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>They also exist in practice as interdisciplinary programmes for mixed chronic pain populations-albeit not usually incorporating manual therapy.<sup><citation rid="R5" ref-type="bibr" count="1">5</citation>,<citation rid="R97" ref-type="bibr" count="1">97</citation></sup> Group formats and peer support are common tools in such programmes and in diabetes care,<sup><citation rid="R30" ref-type="bibr" count="1">30</citation>,<citation rid="R63" ref-type="bibr" count="1">63</citation></sup> with some indication of benefit in DPN and neuropathic pain.<sup><citation rid="R3" ref-type="bibr" count="1">3</citation>,<citation rid="R49" ref-type="bibr" count="1">49</citation>,<citation rid="R69" ref-type="bibr" count="1">69</citation>,<citation rid="R74" ref-type="bibr" count="1">74</citation>,<citation rid="R91" ref-type="bibr" count="1">91</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>Finally, qualitative research underscores the practical intervention limits created by structural barriers, patients' personal needs, and lack of peer support.<citation rid="R74" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>74</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>To maximise population benefit, further intervention development of the NeuOst model may have to consider, first, the specific needs of patient subgroups (eg, socioeconomic, demographic, cultural, disability, and comorbidity differences); second, further adaptations could intensify some intervention components, such as the exercise programme, or add new ones, such as peer support, group sessions, or remote and digitally enabled delivery. <sentence_start/>Adaptations must also enable integration into public healthcare systems. <sentence_start/>While acknowledging limited fidelity monitoring in this trial, we have shown that osteopaths can successfully deliver the intervention. <sentence_start/>We believe this can generalise to other Allied Health Professions with graduate-level training in differential diagnosis, person-centred communication, and nonpharmacological care, assuming completion of the NeuOst training course. <sentence_start/>However, other pathway- and resource-related factors may limit the generalisability to public healthcare systems.<citation rid="R27" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>27</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Further intervention development may thus have to focus on scalable and low-cost intervention components and delivery models. <sentence_start/>Overall, combining physical and psychological intervention components and allowing for person-centred delivery appeared highly promising.
4.4. Limitations

Although our study sample included patients with considerable symptom severity, functional limitations, and comorbidity burden, we did not include people living with amputations or active ulcerations nor with severe mental illness. <sentence_start/>Attending in-person care or participating in physical therapy may not be possible for everyone experiencing such complications and comorbidities.<sup><citation rid="R26" ref-type="bibr" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="R60" ref-type="bibr" count="1">60</citation>,<citation rid="R62" ref-type="bibr" count="1">62</citation>,<citation rid="R82" ref-type="bibr" count="1">82</citation></sup> The intervention was also not specifically adapted to different socioeconomic, cultural, linguistic, age, sex, or gender backgrounds, although intervention development included a diverse group of people and there was flexibility in the programme to accommodate some patient preferences and varying ability levels. <sentence_start/>Importantly, intervention development and this feasibility trial occurred outside a public healthcare system. <sentence_start/>Further stakeholder-driven work is needed here to widen participation and promote implementation of a NeuOst-like programme.

Methodologically, resource constraints led to limited diagnostic procedures and fidelity monitoring, after it emerged that more staff time would be needed for recruitment and data collection than originally expected, making the budget insufficient to fully implement other planned methods. <sentence_start/>Diagnosing neuropathy using only patient report without neurological confirmation may have increased the heterogeneity of the sample. <sentence_start/>In future trials with an explanatory attitude,<citation rid="R42" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>42</sup></citation> neurological examinations may be desirable before enrolment (see section 4.1 of the study protocol for a discussion of the trial along the pragmatic-explanatory spectrum<citation rid="R52" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>52</sup></citation>; accessible at ). <sentence_start/>Alternatively, referral into the study could occur after clinical diagnosis in diabetes or neurology services, thereby also embedding the NeuOst programme into care pathways. <sentence_start/>The lack of our originally planned independent approach to fidelity monitoring through video recordings increases uncertainty, but we judged that this was a manageable risk because specific provider training was provided, supervision by an expert was available, and therapist-reported delivery was high. <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, we recognise that independent fidelity monitoring would have been helpful to better understand intervention delivery and protocol compliance, helping to interpret in particular the comparison of NeuOst to the high-similarity control intervention.
5. <sentence_start/>Conclusion

This feasibility trial demonstrates that a complex, multimodal intervention for people with painful diabetic polyneuropathy can be delivered safely and acceptably by trained Allied Health professionals. <sentence_start/>Despite recruitment challenges and some operational complexities inherent in running a blinded, high-similarity controlled design, key feasibility parameters were met, and participants showed substantial satisfaction and engagement. <sentence_start/>Future work should refine recruitment pathways, streamline outcome measurement, enhance fidelity monitoring, and ensure that active components are clearly differentiated from control conditions. <sentence_start/>Early clinical signals compared with usual care justify progression to a larger trial, although optimisation of the intervention may be useful, including for implementation in public healthcare systems. <sentence_start/>Given the limited efficacy of available pharmacological treatments and the clear patient demand for alternative approaches, a rigorously tested, person-centred multimodal programme such as NeuOst holds meaningful potential to address an important gap in the care of people living with painful diabetic neuropathy.
